data.content_ref: inline:The target's defense is internally contradictory. It claims the preference for better-corroborated theories is 'non-inductive' because it does not assert higher probability, but it simultaneously claims this preference selects theories with 'highest verisimilitude (truth-likeness).' Verisimilitude is a truth-entailing property — claiming a theory is closer to the truth on the basis of how it performed in past tests is structurally identical to claiming it is more probable on the same basis. Both infer a truth-related property from the same evidence (corroboration / survival of severe tests). The target draws a line between 'probability' and 'verisimilitude' but never provides a principled basis for why the inference to one is inductive while the inference to the other is not. The 'methodological rule' framing does not resolve this: a rule that selects theories based on their truth-likeness makes a substantive epistemic claim that corroboration tracks truth-proximity, which is exactly the inductive connection Popper sought to deny. Thus the target smuggles induction back in not merely through its admitted 'metaphysical faith' (objection 1), but through the very concept of verisimilitude it substitutes for probability — the substitute performs the same epistemic work as the thing it replaces.
